15710:
To take exception to something means to strongly object to it or to feel offended by it. When you take exception to something, you are saying, "I disagree with this and I find it unacceptable," or "This bothers me and I won't just let it pass."

Think of it as drawing a line and saying, "No, this is not okay with me."

The word "exception" normally means something that doesn't follow the usual rule — something that is excluded or set apart. When you "take exception" to something, you are mentally setting it apart from what you consider acceptable. You are refusing to let it go unchallenged.

So the full phrase means: "I am singling this out as wrong, offensive, or unacceptable, and I am not going to stay quiet about it."

This idiom carries two closely related but slightly different meanings, and the context usually tells you which one is being used:

1. To strongly disagree with something. This is about objecting to the accuracy or fairness of a statement, claim, or action. You think something is wrong and you want to push back against it.

Example: A manager tells her team that nobody stayed late to finish the project. One employee takes exception to this because she personally stayed until midnight. Here, she is objecting because the statement is factually incorrect.

2. To feel offended or insulted by something. This is more about your feelings being hurt or your dignity feeling attacked. You find something disrespectful or inappropriate.

Example: During a meeting, someone implies that a colleague doesn't care about his work. The colleague takes exception to this because he finds the comment deeply unfair and insulting.

In real life, these two meanings often overlap. When someone says something wrong about you, you can both disagree with it and feel offended by it at the same time. The phrase "take exception to" captures that whole combined reaction beautifully.

The idiom comes from legal language. Centuries ago, in a court of law, a lawyer would formally "take an exception" — that is, they would raise an official objection to something: a piece of evidence, a procedure, or a statement. The lawyer was essentially saying, "I formally mark this as unacceptable."

Over time, this legal habit entered everyday language, and people started using it outside the courtroom to mean any strong objection or sense of being offended.

"Take exception to" is a moderately formal expression. You will hear it more often in:

  • Professional conversations (at work, in meetings)
  • Written communication (emails, articles, formal letters)
  • Debates or serious discussions
  • News commentary and journalism

You will hear it less often in very casual, everyday conversation between friends. In casual speech, people tend to say things like "I have a problem with that," "I disagree," or "that offends me." But "take exception to" is not so formal that it sounds stiff or old-fashioned — it works perfectly well in many everyday professional situations.

The structure is always: take exception to + [something]

The word "to" here is a preposition, not part of an infinitive verb. This means whatever follows "to" must be a noun, a noun phrase, or a gerund (an -ing verb acting as a noun). You cannot follow it with a plain verb.

Study these patterns:

Pattern 1: Take exception to + a noun/noun phrase
She took exception to the decision.
He takes exception to that kind of language.

Pattern 2: Take exception to + someone + verb-ing
I take exception to you speaking to me in that tone.
The director took exception to the journalist misquoting her.

Notice how "speaking" and "misquoting" are gerunds (verb forms acting as nouns). This is correct. You would not say "I take exception to you speak to me like that" — that is grammatically wrong.

Tense flexibility: The idiom works in any tense.

  • Present: "I take exception to this."
  • Past: "She took exception to the comment."
  • Future: "He will take exception to that."

Reading idioms in a variety of contexts is one of the best ways to truly absorb them. Here are several:

In a professional setting:
The senior engineer took exception to the report's conclusion that the team had been careless. He felt the accusation was unfair and untrue, and he said so clearly.

In a personal conversation:
"I have to say, I take exception to the way you described my cooking in front of everyone. It was embarrassing."

In a public debate:
The professor took exception to the journalist's claim that universities no longer promote critical thinking. She argued the exact opposite was true.

In a written statement:
The company issued a formal statement saying it took strong exception to the allegations published in the newspaper.

In a mild, polite way:
"I'll just take exception to one small part of what you said — I don't think the data supports that conclusion."
How It Differs from Similar Expressions

"Take issue with" — This means almost the same thing: to disagree or object. However, "take issue with" is slightly less personal and emotional. It leans more toward intellectual disagreement. "Take exception to" carries a slightly stronger sense of feeling personally offended or challenged.

"Object to" — This is more direct and neutral. It focuses purely on disagreement, without the personal or emotional edge. "Take exception to" implies that you are also somewhat personally bothered.

"Take umbrage at" — This is very similar to "take exception to" in that it also implies feeling offended. However, "take umbrage" is more old-fashioned, more literary, and focuses almost entirely on the offended feeling, with less emphasis on disagreement. "Take exception to" balances both disagreement and offense.

"Be offended by" — This is the everyday, plain version. "Take exception to" is simply a more formal, sophisticated, and precise way of expressing the same emotion combined with objection.

Do not confuse "take exception to" with simply expressing mild dislike. This phrase signals a real, meaningful objection — it has weight and seriousness to it. Using it casually to describe a tiny preference sounds unnatural.

For example, it would sound odd to say: "I take exception to the color they painted the café." That is too trivial a matter. You would normally say "I'm not a fan of" or "I don't love" for minor personal preferences.

Save "take exception to" for situations where you genuinely feel something is wrong, unfair, or offensive — something worth formally pushing back against.

If you want to remember this forever, here it is: "Take exception to" = strongly object to and/or feel offended by. It means something bothers you enough that you feel the need to speak up and say, "No, I don't accept this."
15711:
The Simple Meaning First

"Take in a matinee" means to go and watch a daytime performance — usually an afternoon showing of a movie, a play, a musical, or a similar live or cinematic show.

Example in a sentence:

"We don't have any plans this Saturday afternoon. Want to take in a matinee?"

Translation in plain terms: "Do you want to go watch a movie or show in the afternoon?"

That's the core idea.

The idiom is made of two pieces — "take in" and "matinee" — and both are worth understanding individually.

Part 1: "Take In" (The Phrasal Verb)

"Take in" is a phrasal verb with several different meanings in English, but in this context it means to attend or go to see something for leisure or entertainment. It has a relaxed, casual, almost effortless feel to it — as if you are simply fitting an enjoyable activity into your day.

Think of it like this: you are taking something into your experience — absorbing it, enjoying it, letting it come to you.

Here are more examples of "take in" used in this same way:

  • "We took in a baseball game last Sunday." → We went and watched a baseball game.
  • "She took in a few museums while she was in Paris." → She visited and enjoyed a few museums.
  • "They took in a show on Broadway." → They went to see a Broadway performance.

Notice the tone — it always sounds casual and enjoyable, never like work or obligation. You wouldn't say "I took in a dentist appointment." The phrase implies pleasure and leisure.

Part 2: "Matinee" (The Noun)

The word "matinee" (sometimes spelled matinée, with an accent, because it is borrowed from French) refers to a performance or showing that takes place during the daytime, most commonly in the afternoon.

Where does the word come from?

The word comes from the French word "matin," which means "morning." In French, matinée originally referred to the morning hours or something that happened in the morning. When English borrowed the word, the meaning shifted slightly — in English, a matinee almost always means an afternoon showing, not a morning one, though technically it covers any daytime performance before the evening.

What counts as a matinee?

A matinee can be:

  • An afternoon showing of a movie at a cinema
  • An afternoon performance of a play at a theater
  • An afternoon performance of a musical, opera, or ballet
  • Occasionally, an afternoon concert or sporting event

The key word is daytime — specifically before the typical evening performance time, which is usually around 7:00 or 8:00 PM.

Why do matinees exist?

Theaters and cinemas often schedule matinee performances for practical reasons. Many people — retirees, families with children, tourists, students — are free during the afternoon. Matinees are also typically less crowded than evening shows, and ticket prices are usually cheaper than evening performances. This makes them an attractive option for a relaxed, budget-friendly outing.

So when you combine "take in" (to casually attend something for enjoyment) and "matinee" (a daytime, usually afternoon, performance or showing), you get:

"Take in a matinee" = To casually attend and enjoy an afternoon performance or showing of a movie, play, or similar entertainment.

The full phrase carries a warm, easygoing, and social tone. It suggests a pleasant way to spend an afternoon — not hurried, not formal, just a nice, relaxed outing.

Here are natural sentences to show you how the idiom is used:

  1. "The kids are off school today — let's take in a matinee and grab ice cream after."
  2. "Since we were already downtown, we decided to take in a matinee at the old theater on Fifth Avenue."
  3. "My grandmother and I used to take in a matinee every Friday. It was our little tradition."
  4. "The tickets for the evening show were sold out, so we took in the matinee instead."
  5. "I had the afternoon free, so I took in a matinee of the new action film everyone's been talking about."

This idiom is most commonly used in American English, though it is understood in British English and other varieties as well. It is a slightly old-fashioned or classic-sounding phrase — something you might hear from an older generation or in mid-20th century American films and literature — but it is still in active and perfectly natural use today. It has a charming, timeless quality to it.

These phrases are close cousins in meaning:

  • "Catch a matinee" — Very similar and equally common. "Want to catch a matinee this afternoon?"
  • "See a matinee" — Slightly more literal and direct. "We saw a matinee of the new play."
  • "Go to a matinee" — The most literal version. "Let's go to a matinee."

Of all these, "take in a matinee" sounds the most leisurely and idiomatic. "Catch a matinee" sounds the most casual and modern. "See a matinee" and "go to a matinee" are the most straightforward and literal.

To make sure there is no confusion:

  • It does not mean watching something at home on TV or a screen. It implies going out to a venue.
  • "Take in" here does not mean "to understand" or "to deceive" — two other meanings of "take in" in English. Context always makes it clear which meaning is intended.
  • A matinee is not just any movie or show — it specifically refers to a daytime/afternoon one. An evening showing would simply be called a "show," "evening performance," or "night showing."

"Take in a matinee" = To go out and enjoy an afternoon performance or screening of a movie, play, or similar show — in a relaxed, casual, and pleasurable way.

It's the kind of thing you do on a slow Tuesday afternoon, on a rainy Saturday, or as a gentle, enjoyable tradition with someone you care about. It captures the simple pleasure of stepping away from daily life for a few hours to sit in the dark and be entertained.
15712:
The word "leave" in this idiom does not mean the act of leaving a place (like walking out of a room). Instead, it comes from an old English word meaning "permission." So "take leave" originally meant "take permission to go."

Over centuries of use, this phrase grew into several related meanings. Today, "take leave" appears in three main ways, each slightly different from the others.
Meaning 1: To Say Goodbye to Someone

"Take leave of someone" means to formally or emotionally say goodbye to a person.

This is the classic, oldest meaning. When you "take leave" of someone, you are not just waving and walking away. It carries a sense of a deliberate, often heartfelt farewell — the kind that happens before a long separation, an important departure, or the end of a chapter in life.

Examples:

  • She took leave of her parents at the airport, tears in her eyes.
  • After thirty years at the company, he took leave of his colleagues with a short speech.
  • The soldier took leave of his family before being deployed overseas.

Why "take"? Think of it this way: in the old days, before you could simply leave a gathering or a person's company, you were expected to ask for or formally receive permission to go. That act of receiving permission and departing was called "taking leave." The word "take" suggests that you are claiming or accepting that formal goodbye moment.

Today, we often use it when the goodbye feels significant — not for casual daily partings like "see you tomorrow."
Meaning 2: To Take Authorized Time Off

In formal and professional settings, "take leave" simply means to take approved time away from your work or duties.

You have likely heard phrases like "sick leave," "maternity leave," "casual leave," or "earned leave" — especially in Indian English and British English. When someone "takes leave," they are taking that officially permitted time off.

Examples:

  • She is on leave this week because she is unwell.
  • He applied to take leave for three days to attend a family function.
  • The officer took leave for a month to look after his elderly mother.

This meaning is very common in formal correspondence, HR letters, and official communication. It is essentially the same word "leave" but now used as a noun meaning time off with permission.
Meaning 3: "Take Leave of One's Senses" — To Act Irrationally

This is a fixed expression (a set phrase) that means to suddenly start behaving in a very foolish, wild, or irrational way — as if your mind has gone on a holiday without telling you.

The image behind it is vivid: your senses (your rational mind, your judgment, your common sense) have "departed" just like a person takes leave from work. When someone has taken leave of their senses, their good judgment is simply absent.

Examples:

  • "Have you taken leave of your senses? You can't just quit your job and go live in a forest!"
  • He seemed to have taken leave of his senses when he invested all his savings in a business he knew nothing about.
  • The politician's bizarre speech made many wonder if he had taken leave of his senses.

This expression is typically used in surprise, disbelief, or mild horror at someone's behaviour. It is often rhetorical — meaning the speaker doesn't really think the person is mentally ill, but is expressing shock at a very foolish decision or action.

All three meanings share the same root idea of departure with permission:

FormWhat "departs"?

In the first meaning, you depart from a person — and the act of doing so formally is "taking leave of them."
In the second meaning, you depart from your duties temporarily — that is "taking leave from work."
In the third meaning, your senses (your rational mind) depart from you — so you have "taken leave of your senses."

The common thread: leave = an act of departing, with permission or acknowledgement.

• "Take leave of someone" — formal and literary. You would not say this in casual daily conversation. It sounds mature, serious, and sometimes a little old-fashioned in a dignified way.
  • "Take leave" (from work) — formal and professional. Very standard in official English, especially in South Asian and British contexts.
  • "Take leave of one's senses" — conversational and expressive. Used when someone wants to dramatize their shock at another person's behaviour. It has a slightly humorous edge even when the speaker is genuinely annoyed.
Common Phrases That Use "Leave" in the Same Way

Understanding these will help you see that the idiom is part of a larger family of expressions:

  • "By your leave" — with your permission. (An old-fashioned way of asking permission politely. "May I sit here, by your leave?")
  • "Without so much as a by-your-leave" — without asking anyone's permission; in a very rude or presumptuous way. (He walked into my office and helped himself to my files, without so much as a by-your-leave.)
  • "French leave" — an old idiom for leaving a party or gathering without saying goodbye to the host. (He disappeared halfway through the party — took French leave, as usual.)
  • "On leave" — currently away from work on approved absence.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

"Take leave" comes from an old word meaning permission. It means:

  1. To formally say goodbye to someone (take leave of a person).
  2. To take approved time off from work (take leave from your duties).
  3. To behave irrationally, as if your mind has gone absent (take leave of your senses).

The unifying idea across all uses: something — you, your time, or your reason — departs with a kind of formal acknowledgement.
15713:
When you take your cue from someone, you watch what that person does (or says) and use it as your guide for what you should do next. You treat their behavior as a signal, a hint, or an example that tells you how to act.

In the simplest possible terms: they move first, and you follow their lead.

This idiom was born in the world of theatre.

In a stage play, actors don't just say their lines randomly. They wait for a specific moment — a specific word, a gesture, or a sound — that signals it's their turn to speak or move. That signal is called a cue.

For example, an actor might be told: "Your cue to walk on stage is when the other actor says the word 'tomorrow'." The moment that word is spoken, the actor knows — now I move.

So a cue is a trigger signal that tells you when and how to act.

Over time, this theatrical idea traveled out of the theatre and into everyday life. People started using "take your cue from someone" to mean: watch that person carefully, treat their behavior as your signal, and act accordingly.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

• Take — to receive or adopt something
  • One's cue — the signal meant for you
  • From someone — the source of that signal is another person

Put it together: you receive your signal — your direction — from another person.
The Core Idea (The Heart of the Idiom)

There are two important things happening when someone "takes their cue" from another person:

  1. Observation — You are watching someone else carefully.
  2. Imitation or response — You then adjust your own behavior based on what you saw.

You are essentially saying: "I don't know exactly what to do here, so I'll look at what this other person is doing and use that as my roadmap."

The person you take your cue from is usually:

  • someone more experienced than you
  • someone in a position of authority
  • someone who knows the situation better
  • or simply someone who acts first in a moment of uncertainty

Example 1:

"It was my first day at the new job. I didn't know when we were supposed to take lunch breaks, so I took my cue from my colleagues and went when they went."

→ The speaker had no idea what the routine was, so they watched their coworkers and copied their behavior to fit in.

Example 2:

"The children took their cue from their teacher and sat down quietly when the guest speaker entered the room."

→ The children saw the teacher sit down quietly, understood that as a signal, and did the same.

Example 3:

"As a young designer, she took her cue from the great architects of the 20th century, building her style around their principles."

→ Here, she isn't responding to a live signal. Instead, she used their work as inspiration and a guide for developing her own approach. This is a broader, more figurative use.

Example 4:

"He noticed his host picking up the smallest fork first, so he took his cue from him and did the same."

→ A classic social situation — uncertain about etiquette, he watched someone more confident and mirrored their action.

This idiom is flexible. Depending on the situation, it can carry slightly different flavors:

1. Following in uncertainty
When you don't know what to do, you look to someone who seems to know and follow them. (Like the new employee example above.)

2. Learning from a role model
You admire someone and consciously model your behavior, style, or decisions on theirs over a long period of time. (Like the designer example above.)

3. Responding to a social signal
Someone does something — maybe they laugh, stand up, lower their voice, or start leaving — and you pick up on that as a cue to do the same. This is very close to the original theatrical meaning.

4. Adapting based on someone's reaction
Sometimes you watch how an audience or group reacts and adjust accordingly.

"The comedian took his cue from the audience's silence and moved on to a different joke."

In all four cases, the structure is the same: observe → receive the signal → act accordingly.

It's important to know what this idiom doesn't mean, so you don't confuse it with similar ideas:

  • It does not mean mindlessly copying someone without thought. It implies a conscious, deliberate choice to follow someone's lead.
  • It is not the same as "taking orders from someone." Cues are signals you choose to follow; orders are commands you are told to obey.
  • It does not require the other person to be intentionally giving you a signal. Sometimes the person doesn't even know you are watching them and taking your cue from them.

The idiom appears in many forms in real usage:

VariationExample
take one's cue from"Take your cue from the experts."
took his/her/their cue from"She took her cue from the senior staff."
taking a cue from"Taking a cue from nature, the engineer redesigned the bridge."
took a cue from"He took a cue from the way his father handled pressure."

(Note: "a cue" and "one's cue" are both correct and mean essentially the same thing in this idiom.)

Picture yourself as an actor frozen on a dark stage. You don't know when to move. Then another actor says a certain word — your cue — and you spring into action.

That's exactly what this idiom means in real life: you are waiting, watching, and the moment someone gives you a signal through their actions or behavior, you move.

"Take one's cue from someone" means to watch what another person does and use their behavior as a guide or signal for your own actions — especially in moments of uncertainty, in learning situations, or in social settings where you want to fit in or follow the right lead.
15714:
"Take out" is a phrasal verb — a verb ("take") combined with a small word ("out") that together create a new meaning, often very different from the original verb. English has hundreds of these, and they confuse learners because the words alone don't tell you the meaning.

The tricky thing about "take out" is that it has many different meanings depending on the situation. This is completely normal in English. Context is your guide.

1. To remove something from inside a place or container

This is the most basic and literal meaning. You physically move something from inside to outside.

  • "She opened her bag and took out her phone."
  • "Please take out the trash before you go to bed."
  • "He took out a pen and started writing."
  • "The dentist took out two of my teeth."

Think of it like this: something is in somewhere → you move it out. Simple.

2. To bring someone somewhere as a social activity (usually paying for them)

When you "take someone out," you invite them to go somewhere — a restaurant, a movie, a show — and you typically pay for them. It's an act of generosity or romance.

  • "He took her out to dinner for their anniversary."
  • "My boss took the whole team out for lunch."
  • "I want to take you out this weekend — my treat."

Notice that you always "take someone out." The person you're taking is always mentioned.

3. Food you order at a restaurant to eat elsewhere (not inside the restaurant)

In this meaning, "takeout" (also written "take-out" or "take away" in British English) is a noun referring to food ordered from a restaurant but eaten at home or somewhere else. You can also use "take out" as a verb here.

  • "Let's just order takeout tonight. I don't want to cook."
  • "Can I take this out, please?" (asking the restaurant to pack the food to go)
  • "They sell great takeout food."

In British English and many other varieties, people say "takeaway" instead of "takeout," but the meaning is exactly the same.

4. To obtain something officially (a loan, insurance, a license, etc.)

When you formally apply for and receive something from a bank, government, or institution, you "take it out." This is very common in financial and legal contexts.

  • "They took out a loan to buy their house."
  • "You should take out travel insurance before the trip."
  • "She took out a membership at the gym."
  • "He took out a patent on his invention."

The idea here is that you are extracting something from a system by going through a formal process.

5. To withdraw money

Specifically for money, "take out" means to remove cash from a bank account, usually from an ATM.

  • "I need to take out some cash before we go."
  • "She took out ₹5,000 from the ATM."

6. To destroy, defeat, or eliminate something (military/action contexts)

In military language, news reports, action movies, and games, "take out" means to destroy or eliminate a target — a vehicle, a weapon, a building, or even a person.

  • "The soldiers were ordered to take out the enemy's radar station."
  • "The missile took out the bridge."
  • "In the game, your mission is to take out the final boss."

This meaning is powerful and direct, and it deliberately avoids more graphic language.

7. To take your feelings out on someone (always used with "on")

This specific pattern — "take it out on" someone — means to direct your anger, frustration, or bad mood toward someone who didn't cause it. You're using an innocent person as a target for your negative emotions.

  • "He had a terrible day at work and took it out on his family."
  • "Don't take it out on me — I didn't do anything wrong."
  • "She was upset about the news but tried not to take it out on anyone."

Notice the structure is always: take + it/your frustration/your anger + out + on + person.

8. To take something out of something (extracting or removing from a source)

Sometimes "take out" refers to removing something from within a larger thing — a word, a scene, a stain, a clause.

  • "The editor took out several paragraphs from the article."
  • "Can you take out this stain from my shirt?"
  • "The director decided to take out the last scene from the movie."

This is closely related to meaning #1 but is used for less physical, more abstract removals.
A Quick Summary of All Meanings

Here's the full picture in plain words:

Take out = remove physically → take out your wallet
Take out = bring someone somewhere socially → take her out to dinner
Take out = food to go → order takeout
Take out = obtain formally → take out a loan
Take out = withdraw cash → take out money
Take out = destroy a target → take out the enemy
Take it out on = vent emotions wrongly → take it out on someone
Take out = remove from within → take out a scene
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

You almost never need to guess, because the surrounding words make it clear every time.

  • If there's a person being taken somewhere enjoyable → it's the social meaning.
  • If there's a bank, loan, or insurance nearby → it's the formal/financial meaning.
  • If it's in a military or game context → it's the destroy meaning.
  • If you see "on" after it → it's the emotional venting meaning.
  • If it's about food → it's the takeout meaning.

"Take out" can be separated when you use it with an object:

  • "Take it out." ✅
  • "Take out it." ❌ (wrong when using a pronoun)
  • "Take out the trash." ✅
  • "Take the trash out." ✅ (both word orders are fine with nouns)

When a pronoun like "it," "them," or "him" is the object, it must go in the middle: take it out, never take out it.

That's everything you need to know about "take out" — every major meaning, every context, the grammar rule, and how to tell them apart.
15715:
1. The Simple Meaning

When someone "takes over the baton," it means they accept a responsibility, role, or task from another person and continue it forward.

Think of it this way: someone else started something — a project, a job, a mission, a tradition — and now you are the one stepping in to carry it on.
2. Where Does It Come From? (The Origin)

To truly understand this idiom, you need to picture a relay race in athletics (track and field).

In a relay race, a team of runners — usually four — take turns running portions of the race. Each runner doesn't run the whole distance alone. Instead, they carry a small, smooth, cylindrical stick called a baton. When one runner finishes their portion, they physically hand the baton to the next runner, who then sprints forward with it. This continues until the last runner crosses the finish line.

The baton is the symbol of the ongoing effort. As long as someone is holding it and running with it, the race continues. The moment the baton is dropped, the team is in trouble.

This is exactly what the idiom captures: the baton = the responsibility, the work, or the mission. Just like in a relay race, life, business, and society often require one person to finish their part and hand things off to the next person, who then takes over and keeps going.
3. Breaking Down the Phrase Word by Word

• Take over — to assume control of something; to start doing something that someone else was doing before you.
  • The baton — borrowed from the relay race; symbolically represents the duty, role, task, or cause being passed on.

Together: "Take over the baton" = step in and continue what someone else has been doing.
4. The Full Family of Related Expressions

This idiom appears in several closely related forms. They all share the same core meaning but describe the action from a different person's point of view:

"Pass the baton" — told from the perspective of the person giving the responsibility. The outgoing person is the focus.

The retiring CEO passed the baton to her deputy.

"Hand over the baton" — similar to "pass the baton," but slightly more deliberate and ceremonious in tone.

The founder handed over the baton after 30 years.

"Take over the baton" — told from the perspective of the person receiving the responsibility. The incoming person is the focus.

The new manager took over the baton and led the team brilliantly.

"Pick up the baton" — this one has a slightly different nuance. It suggests the new person is stepping up, sometimes when the previous person could not finish, or when the role needs someone to grab it with energy and determination.

When the lead scientist retired unexpectedly, her student picked up the baton and completed the research.

"Carry the baton" — focuses on the act of continuing the work over time, rather than the moment of transfer.

She carried the baton of her father's human rights activism throughout her entire career.

All these variations come from the same relay race image. Learning them together helps you understand the full picture.
5. What Does It Imply? (The Deeper Tone)

This idiom carries some important emotional weight beneath the surface:

  • It implies continuity — something is being kept alive, not abandoned.
  • It implies trust — the person passing the baton trusts the new person to do it well.
  • It implies responsibility — the person receiving the baton is expected to take it seriously and not let things fall apart.
  • It implies a chain of effort — one person's work builds on another's. No one person does everything alone.

This is why the idiom is often used in meaningful or important contexts — leadership, causes, family legacies, organizations — rather than trivial everyday tasks.
6. Real-Life Contexts Where You Will Hear This

In business and leadership:

After leading the company for two decades, the chairman took over the baton from the original founder and steered it into the digital era.

In politics:

The new president took over the baton of economic reform and promised to continue the policies of the previous administration.

In family and tradition:

When her grandmother passed away, Sofia took over the baton of running the family bakery that had existed for over a century.

In social causes and activism:

A new generation of climate activists took over the baton from the pioneers who started the movement in the 1970s.

In science and academia:

After the professor retired, his most talented student took over the baton of the groundbreaking neurological research.

In sports (beyond literal relay racing):

When the team captain was injured, the vice-captain took over the baton of leadership and guided the squad to the championship.

It's important to know what this idiom does not imply, so you don't misuse it:

  • It does not mean simply starting something brand new from scratch. There must be a predecessor — someone who came before and did the work first.
  • It does not mean stealing or taking something against someone's will. The transfer is generally understood to be natural, voluntary, or necessary.
  • It does not apply to very small or trivial tasks in most formal writing. You wouldn't normally say "she took over the baton of making morning tea." For important, ongoing duties — yes. For minor, one-off tasks — it sounds out of place.

This idiom is neutral to slightly formal. You will find it comfortably in:

  • Newspaper articles and journalism
  • Business speeches and corporate communication
  • Formal writing and essays
  • Everyday conversation when the topic is serious or significant

It is not slang. It is polished, recognized, and respected across English-speaking cultures worldwide.

If you ever forget this idiom's meaning, just close your eyes and picture a relay race:

Four runners. One baton. Runner 1 sprints, then hands it to Runner 2, who sprints, then hands it to Runner 3… and so on.

The baton never stops moving. The work never stops moving. Someone always takes it and keeps going.

That image is the idiom.
"Take over the baton" means to step into someone else's role, duty, or ongoing effort — and carry it forward with the same dedication they showed, or better.
15716:
To take something in stride means to handle a difficult, surprising, or unpleasant situation calmly, without panicking, complaining, or losing focus. When someone takes something in stride, they don't let it disturb their peace of mind or stop them from moving forward. They simply deal with it quietly and keep going.

Think of it this way: imagine you are walking. If you step on a small stone, you don't fall down and cry about it — you just adjust your step slightly and continue walking. That is exactly the spirit of this idiom. You face the problem, you absorb it, and you move on without making a big deal of it.

The idiom comes from horse racing and equestrian (horse-riding) sports.

A horse moves in a rhythmic pattern of steps called a stride. When a horse encounters an obstacle — like a fence or a hurdle — a well-trained horse clears that obstacle without breaking its rhythm. It jumps over smoothly, lands, and continues galloping at the same pace. It doesn't stumble, panic, or slow down. It takes the obstacle within its stride — as if the obstacle were just a normal part of the run.

This image was borrowed into everyday English to describe people who handle life's obstacles in the same smooth, uninterrupted way.

This is important: taking something in stride does not mean:

  • Pretending the problem doesn't exist
  • Being careless or indifferent
  • Suppressing your feelings completely

It does mean:

  • You acknowledge the difficulty
  • But you don't overreact to it
  • You stay composed and level-headed
  • You handle it and keep moving forward

The key feeling is calm resilience — a quiet inner strength that lets you face challenges without being thrown off balance.

There is a small difference in the two main varieties of English:

  • American English: "Take something in stride"
  • British English: "Take something in one's stride"

Both mean exactly the same thing. The only difference is the word "one's" in the British version. You may see either form depending on what you are reading.

The structure is:

take + [the thing/problem] + in stride

The verb "take" changes based on tense, just like any normal verb:

TenseExample
PresentShe takes criticism in stride.
PastHe took the bad news in stride.
FutureI'm sure she'll take it in stride.
Present continuousHe is taking all of this in stride.

"In stride" itself never changes. It always stays exactly as it is.

Here are examples showing the idiom used in different situations. Read each one and notice the feeling of calm acceptance in each:

1. Bad news at work:

"When the manager told him his project was cancelled, he took it in stride and immediately asked what he could work on next."

(He was not devastated or angry. He accepted it and moved forward.)

2. A sports setback:

"The team lost three games in a row, but the players took it in stride and trained harder for the next match."

(They didn't fall apart emotionally. They accepted the losses and stayed focused.)

3. A personal challenge:

"Moving to a new country was not easy, but she took it all in stride — the new language, the new culture, everything."

(She adapted to difficulties without excessive stress or complaint.)

4. Unexpected problems:

"The flight was cancelled, and he just took it in stride — he found another flight and used the waiting time to get some work done."

(An annoyance that might upset many people didn't upset him at all.)

5. In conversation (complimenting someone):

"I don't know how she does it — she takes everything in stride. Nothing seems to rattle her."

(Here, someone is admiring another person's calm nature.)
What Kind of Person "Takes Things in Stride"?

When someone is described as a person who takes things in stride, people are complimenting them. It means:

  • They are emotionally mature
  • They are resilient (they bounce back quickly)
  • They are not a drama-maker
  • They have a stable, grounded personality
  • They know how to prioritize what matters and not waste energy on panic

It is almost always used as a positive quality.

These idioms and expressions carry a very similar idea, so knowing them will help you understand the concept more deeply:

  • "Roll with the punches" — adapt to difficulties as they come (from boxing)
  • "Keep your cool" — stay calm under pressure
  • "Not miss a beat" — continue without being disrupted
  • "Handle it with grace" — deal with something in a composed, dignified way
  • "Keep calm and carry on" — a popular saying meaning to stay composed and continue

QuestionAnswer
What does it mean?Handle a difficulty calmly and keep moving forward
Is it positive or negative?Always positive — it's a compliment
Does it mean ignoring the problem?No — it means handling it without overreacting
Where does it come from?Horse racing — a horse clearing a jump without breaking stride
British version?"Take something in one's stride"
One Final Way to Remember It Forever

Picture a professional surfer. A wave comes crashing toward them — powerful and potentially dangerous. An amateur panics and wipes out. But the professional reads the wave, adjusts, and rides it smoothly. They didn't avoid the wave. They didn't pretend it wasn't there. They simply took it in stride.

That surfer is the perfect image of this idiom.
15717:
"Take the edge off" means to reduce the intensity of something unpleasant — not to remove it completely, but to make it slightly less painful, less stressful, less strong, or less difficult to deal with.

Think of it this way: imagine a sharp knife. The edge is the sharpest, most intense part of it. If you "take the edge off," you dull that sharpness a little. The knife is still there — but it doesn't cut as harshly anymore.

That image is the soul of this idiom. The "edge" = the worst, most intense part of something bad. "Taking it off" = softening that intensity.
The Core Idea in One Sentence

Something eases the worst part of a bad feeling or situation — without making it disappear entirely.

This "something" could be food, a drink, music, a conversation, medicine, humor, or anything else that brings even a little relief.

The idiom comes from the literal world of blades and tools. A blade with a sharp edge cuts powerfully and aggressively. When you blunt or dull that edge, it becomes less severe.

Over centuries, English speakers began using "edge" as a metaphor for the sharpest, most biting part of a bad experience — like the edge of pain, hunger, fear, or anger. And "taking it off" meant softening that intensity.

The phrase has been used in English since at least the 1500s in various forms, and it remains in common use today across the world.
What Kinds of "Edges" Can Be Taken Off?

This idiom is very flexible. It is used in many different situations:

1. Physical pain or discomfort
A painkiller doesn't always cure pain — it just makes it more bearable.

"The ibuprofen didn't cure my headache, but it took the edge off."

2. Hunger
A small snack before a big meal reduces how desperately hungry you feel.

"I ate a few crackers to take the edge off before dinner."

3. Stress or anxiety
Something that helps you calm down a little when you're overwhelmed.

"Listening to music after work really takes the edge off."

4. Sadness or grief
Something that makes a painful emotion slightly easier to carry.

"Talking to a friend took the edge off the sadness he felt after the loss."

5. Anger
Something that cools your temper a little before you react.

"She took a few deep breaths to take the edge off her frustration before the meeting."

6. Cold or heat
Physical discomfort from weather can also be softened.

"A warm coat took the edge off the freezing wind."
"A cold glass of water took the edge off the afternoon heat."

7. Boredom or awkwardness
Something that makes a dull or uncomfortable situation a little more tolerable.

"His humor took the edge off the awkward silence in the room."
What "Taking the Edge Off" Does NOT Mean

This is very important. The idiom does not mean the problem is solved or gone. It only means the worst part has been softened.

  • It does not mean you feel great.
  • It does not mean the pain, stress, or problem has disappeared.
  • It means you feel slightly better than you did before — just enough to cope.

Think of it like turning down the volume on loud, painful music. The music is still playing — but it's not as unbearable now.
The Grammar: How Is It Used?

The most common structure is:

Something + takes the edge off + (something)

The second "something" (the problem) is often left out when it's already clear from context.

  • "A hot cup of tea really takes the edge off." ✅ (We understand — it takes the edge off the cold, or the stress, etc.)
  • "A hot cup of tea takes the edge off the cold." ✅ (Fully stated)

You can also say:

  • "Take the edge off of something" — especially in American English.
    "This music helps take the edge off of my anxiety."
  • "Takes the edge off things" — a general, non-specific use.
    "A short walk takes the edge off things after a long day."
Tone and Feel of the Idiom

This idiom has a calm, everyday, realistic tone. It is not dramatic. It doesn't promise miracles. It simply acknowledges that life has hard edges — and sometimes, we find small ways to make them softer.

It is used in:

  • Casual conversation ✅
  • Formal writing (less common, but acceptable) ✅
  • Medical or professional contexts ✅
    "This medication may take the edge off the discomfort during recovery."

It is not rude, not slang, and not offensive in any way. It is a neutral, widely accepted idiom.
A Note on Alcohol and This Idiom

You will often hear this idiom connected to drinking alcohol:

"I had a glass of wine to take the edge off after a stressful day."

This is a very common usage, but it is just one example of the idiom — not its only meaning. The idiom itself is completely general and applies to any kind of relief, not just alcohol. Don't let this association limit your understanding of the phrase.

These phrases share a similar meaning and can often be used in the same situations:

  • "Ease the pain" — reduce emotional or physical suffering
  • "Soften the blow" — make bad news or a difficult event less shocking
  • "Dull the pain" — reduce the intensity of pain (physical or emotional)
  • "Take the sting out of something" — remove the most hurtful part of something
  • "Lighten the load" — make a burden feel less heavy

The difference is that "take the edge off" is the most versatile and widely used among these. It works for pain, stress, hunger, cold, boredom, and more.

QuestionAnswer
What does it mean?To reduce the worst intensity of something unpleasant
Does the problem disappear?No — it just becomes more bearable
What can it apply to?Pain, stress, hunger, cold, anger, sadness, boredom
Is it formal or informal?Both — widely used in all contexts
What's the key image?Dulling the sharp edge of a blade

The beauty of this idiom is its honesty. It doesn't say things are fixed or perfect. It simply says: something helped, even if just a little — and sometimes, that little bit is exactly what we need.
15718:
To take the initiative means to act on your own, without waiting to be told, asked, or pushed by someone else. You see something that needs to be done — or an opportunity worth grabbing — and you go ahead and do it yourself, first, without prompting.

A simple way to feel it: imagine a problem sitting in a room. Everyone can see it. Most people wait for someone else to solve it. The person who takes the initiative walks up and starts solving it — not because they were assigned to, but because they decided to.
Breaking Down the Words

Initiative (noun) comes from the Latin word initium, meaning a beginning. So "initiative" means "the act of beginning something." Over time, it also came to mean the energy, drive, or willingness to begin — a quality that lives inside a person.

When someone says "she has initiative," they mean she's the type of person who starts things on her own, without needing to be told.

Take here means to claim or grab something for yourself. You are taking ownership of the action.

Put together: to take the initiative = to claim for yourself the role of the person who starts, acts, or moves first.
The Full Picture: What the Phrase Really Means

The phrase goes beyond just "doing something." It carries several layers:

1. You acted first.
You didn't wait for someone else to go ahead and then follow. You were the one who moved. This is the most essential part.

2. Nobody told you to.
There was no instruction, no request, no order. You identified what needed to happen on your own and acted on that judgement.

3. You took responsibility.
By acting first without being asked, you took ownership. You are now accountable for what you started. That takes courage and confidence.

4. You were proactive, not reactive.
Reactive means: something happens to you, and then you respond.
Proactive means: you decide what to do before anything pushes you to.
Taking the initiative is the ultimate proactive move.
Where the Phrase Comes From

The phrase has strong roots in military strategy. In battle, the side that "holds the initiative" controls when, where, and how the fight happens. They are setting the pace. The other side is constantly reacting, always a step behind.

A general who "takes the initiative" attacks before the enemy can prepare — forcing the enemy to react rather than act. This gives an enormous strategic advantage.

Over centuries, this military concept spread into everyday life — business, sports, relationships, and personal growth — because the underlying truth is universal: the person or group that moves first, moves on their own terms.
How It Is Used in a Sentence

The phrase is very flexible. Here are the main patterns:

Take the initiative (by doing something):
"When she saw no one had organised the meeting, she took the initiative and sent the invitations herself."

Take the initiative (without specifying what was done):
"I appreciated that he took the initiative. Without him, nothing would have happened."

Show initiative / Use initiative (closely related):
"Good employees show initiative."
"Use your initiative — figure it out yourself."

Have the initiative (mostly in military/strategy contexts):
"Our team had the initiative in the second half of the match."

On someone's own initiative:
"No one asked her; she did it on her own initiative."

Note: "take the initiative" is usually followed by "and + verb" or "to + verb" when you want to explain what was done:

  • "He took the initiative and called the client."
  • "She took the initiative to resolve the conflict."
Real-Life Examples Across Different Contexts

At work:
Your team is behind on a project. The manager hasn't said anything yet. You take the initiative — you create a schedule, divide the tasks, and share it with everyone before the meeting. Nobody told you to do that. You saw the problem and solved it.

In a friendship:
Your group of friends hasn't met in months. Everyone is thinking about it but nobody does anything. You take the initiative — you pick a date, choose a place, and send the message. The reunion happens because of you.

In learning:
Your teacher only teaches what's in the textbook. But you notice a topic you're curious about. Instead of waiting to be taught, you take the initiative — you read extra books, watch videos, and learn it yourself.

In conflict:
Two colleagues are not speaking after a disagreement. The tension is hurting the whole team. One of them takes the initiative — she walks up to the other, says "Let's talk this through," and they resolve it. She didn't wait for the other person to come first.

In a crisis:
There is a small fire in an office kitchen. Everyone freezes. One person takes the initiative, grabs the fire extinguisher, and puts it out. They didn't wait for the fire warden to arrive.
What It Looks Like NOT to Take the Initiative

Understanding the opposite helps sharpen the meaning.

Not taking the initiative looks like:

  • Waiting for someone to give you instructions before you act
  • Seeing a problem but doing nothing because "it's not your job"
  • Waiting for someone else to go first so you don't have to take the risk
  • Saying "I didn't know what to do, so I did nothing"
  • Watching an opportunity pass because you hesitated

People who consistently don't take the initiative are often described as passive, reactive, or waiting to be told what to do.
What Taking the Initiative Says About a Person

When we say someone "takes the initiative," we are almost always complimenting them. The phrase implies:

  • Confidence — they trust their own judgment enough to act without approval
  • Responsibility — they are willing to own the outcome
  • Awareness — they notice things that need doing
  • Drive — they don't need external motivation; it comes from within
  • Leadership — even without a formal title, they lead by acting first

This is why interviewers, teachers, coaches, and managers often look for people who "show initiative." It signals that this person doesn't need to be constantly managed or pushed — they move on their own.
A Nuance: Can Taking the Initiative Ever Be Wrong?

Yes, occasionally. Taking the initiative assumes you have enough understanding of the situation to act wisely. If you act too quickly, without enough information, you might overstep, make a mistake, or take over something that wasn't yours to handle.

For example: your colleague is carefully working on a delicate negotiation. You "take the initiative" and email the other party with your own proposal, disrupting everything. Here, acting first without checking wasn't bold — it was careless.

So the phrase is positive when the action is well-judged, and problematic when the action is rash or overreaching. In most everyday usage, however, "taking the initiative" is praised.
Related Phrases Worth Knowing

These phrases live in the same neighbourhood as "take the initiative":

  • "Be proactive" — actively create situations rather than just responding to them (same spirit, more modern business language)
  • "Step up" — come forward and take responsibility when needed
  • "Take the bull by the horns" — tackle a difficult problem directly and boldly
  • "Take charge" — assume control of a situation
  • "Show initiative" — demonstrate that you can act without being told (used to describe a quality, not a single act)
  • "On one's own initiative" — doing something without being asked (emphasises the self-starting quality)
  • "Seize the moment" — recognise and act on an opportunity before it passes
One-Line Summary to Lock It In

"Take the initiative" means: to act first, on your own judgment, without waiting to be told — because you saw what needed to happen and you chose to make it happen yourself.

That is everything you will ever need to know about this phrase — its meaning, its roots, how it's used, what it implies, and when it applies. You have it completely.
15719:
A talisman is a physical object — usually small enough to carry or wear — that a person believes holds a special, magical, or supernatural power. That power is thought to do something beneficial for its owner: bring good luck, attract success, offer protection, grant strength, or ward off bad things.

The single most important thing to understand about a talisman is this: the power is believed to live inside the object itself. It's not just a reminder of something good. It's not just a decoration. According to the belief surrounding it, the object is the source of the power.

Imagine you found a small, old coin. Someone tells you, "This coin has a special energy — whoever carries it will have good fortune." You start carrying it everywhere. Before a big exam, before a job interview, before a game — you hold it and feel confident. That coin, in this belief, is a talisman.

It could be a stone, a ring, a pendant, a carved figure, a piece of cloth, a symbol written on paper, or virtually anything. What makes it a talisman is not what it's made of, but what it is believed to do.
What a Talisman Is Believed to Do

Talismans are generally believed to serve one or more of these purposes:

  • Attract good things — luck, love, wealth, success, health, fertility
  • Repel bad things — evil, danger, sickness, bad luck, curses
  • Grant power or ability — courage, strength, wisdom, victory

A single talisman usually has a specific purpose tied to it. An ancient warrior might carry one talisman for victory in battle and another for protection from arrows — not one object for everything.
How Talismans Are Typically Made or Obtained

This matters because a talisman isn't just any random object. In traditional belief systems, a talisman's power usually comes from:

  • Being crafted from specific materials (gold, silver, certain stones, bones, wood from a sacred tree)
  • Being made or blessed at a specific time (during a full moon, at sunrise, during a religious ceremony)
  • Having symbols, words, or prayers inscribed on it (sacred texts, magical symbols, divine names)
  • Being blessed or consecrated by a spiritual authority (a priest, a shaman, a holy person)

This process is what separates a talisman from just a random pretty stone. The ritual or the belief system charges the object with meaning and supposed power.
Real-World Examples Through History and Cultures

Talismans have appeared in virtually every human civilization in history:

  • Ancient Egypt: The scarab beetle was one of the most famous talismans, believed to bring protection, good luck, and rebirth.
  • Medieval Europe: People wore small pouches containing herbs, written prayers, or sacred bones, believing they provided divine protection.
  • Islamic tradition: Verses from the Quran are sometimes written on paper or metal and worn or kept in homes for protection and blessing.
  • East Asian cultures: Carved jade pieces, certain coins with square holes, and specific symbols are kept as objects of good fortune.
  • The Hamsa (Hand of Fatima): A hand-shaped symbol used across Middle Eastern and North African cultures, believed to protect against the "evil eye."
  • Sports culture: An athlete who always wears the same wristband because they won their biggest game wearing it — in their mind, it's their talisman.

Since you'll encounter related words, here's how they compare:

Talisman vs. Amulet
These two words are so close that people — even dictionaries — often use them as if they mean the same thing. But there is a traditional distinction worth knowing:

  • A talisman is generally thought to actively attract good things (luck, love, success, power).
  • An amulet is generally thought to passively protect against bad things (evil, curses, harm, illness).

Think of it this way: a talisman is like a magnet pulling good things toward you; an amulet is like a shield blocking bad things from reaching you. In practice, however, these lines blur heavily, and many objects serve both roles.

Talisman vs. Charm
A "charm" is a broader word. It can refer to a spoken spell, a sung incantation, or a physical object. When it's a physical object (like a "lucky charm"), it overlaps significantly with a talisman. The word "charm" also tends to feel more casual and everyday, while "talisman" often carries a slightly more serious, ancient, or mystical tone.

Talisman vs. Idol
An idol is an image or statue representing a god or deity — it's an object of worship. A talisman, by contrast, is an object of use — you carry it or keep it near you to gain benefit from it. You don't necessarily pray to a talisman; you rely on its supposed power.

In modern everyday language, the word "talisman" is also used figuratively — meaning it's used to describe something that brings luck or confidence even without any literal belief in magic.

For example:

  • "His grandfather's old watch became his talisman — he wore it to every important meeting."
  • "The team's worn-out jersey was their talisman; they hadn't lost a game while wearing it."

Here, nobody is claiming the watch or jersey contains supernatural power. But psychologically, the object gives the person a feeling of strength, calm, or confidence. The word "talisman" is used to capture that powerful personal significance.
The One Idea That Ties It All Together

Whether ancient or modern, religious or superstitious, literal or figurative — a talisman always comes down to this single core idea:

An object that is believed to hold power, and that power benefits the person connected to it.

The object earns the name "talisman" not because of what it is made of, but because of what someone truly believes it does.
